Monotony and strain

Source: vignettes/articles/monotony-strain.Rmd
monotony-strain.Rmd
library(trainingmodels)

Theory

Session RPE load (Foster 1998; Foster et al. 2001; MODELS.md, M-10). The load of a session is its rating of perceived exertion multiplied by its duration:

w=RPE×D w = \mathrm{RPE} \times D

The RPE is one global rating of the whole session on the 0-10 category-ratio scale, asked about 30 minutes after the session ends. The duration DD is in minutes and covers the entire session, including warm-up, cool-down and recovery intervals. Sessions of the same day are summed, so each day has one load.

Monotony and strain (Foster 1998; MODELS.md, M-12). For the daily loads of a week,

monotony=mean daily loadSD of the daily loads,strain=weekly load×monotony. \text{monotony} = \frac{\text{mean daily load}}{\text{SD of the daily loads}}, \qquad \text{strain} = \text{weekly load} \times \text{monotony}.

The standard deviation is the sample standard deviation (divisor n−1n - 1). Monotony is high when the loads of the week are similar to each other; strain combines the amount of training with its monotony.

The package computes both over a rolling window of window days (7 by default), every day. The argument same_day_load chooses whether the window ends on the current day ("include", the default) or on the previous day ("exclude"). Rest days count as load 0. A window that contains a missing day gives NA. When all loads of a window are equal the standard deviation is 0, and monotony and strain are NA.

Sources: Foster C (1998). Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, 30(7), 1164-1168. Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, et al. (2001). A new approach to monitoring exercise training. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 15(1), 109-115.

Computation

Foster (1998, Table 1) gives one week of training with the duration and the RPE of each day.

week <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date("2026-01-04") + 0:6,
  duration = c(180, 120, 20, 90, 75, 20, 120),
  rpe = c(5, 7, 2, 6, 7, 2, 7)
)
week$load <- srpe_load(week$rpe, week$duration)
week
#>         date duration rpe load
#> 1 2026-01-04      180   5  900
#> 2 2026-01-05      120   7  840
#> 3 2026-01-06       20   2   40
#> 4 2026-01-07       90   6  540
#> 5 2026-01-08       75   7  525
#> 6 2026-01-09       20   2   40
#> 7 2026-01-10      120   7  840

The daily loads are 900, 840, 40, 540, 525, 40 and 840, as in the table. They are turned into a daily series and described with a 7-day window:

x <- as_daily_load(week, date = "date", load = "load")
out <- monotony_strain(x, window = 7)
out
#>   athlete       date load window_load mean_load  sd_load monotony   strain
#> 1       1 2026-01-04  900          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 2       1 2026-01-05  840          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 3       1 2026-01-06   40          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 4       1 2026-01-07  540          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 5       1 2026-01-08  525          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 6       1 2026-01-09   40          NA        NA       NA       NA       NA
#> 7       1 2026-01-10  840        3725  532.1429 367.2857 1.448853 5396.976

Only the seventh day has a complete window. Its values agree with the printed ones:

day7 <- out[7, ]
data.frame(
  quantity = c("Weekly load", "Mean daily load", "SD", "Monotony", "Strain"),
  printed = c(3725, 532, 367, 1.44, 5397),
  package = c(day7$window_load, day7$mean_load, day7$sd_load,
              day7$monotony, day7$strain)
)
#>          quantity printed     package
#> 1     Weekly load 3725.00 3725.000000
#> 2 Mean daily load  532.00  532.142857
#> 3              SD  367.00  367.285733
#> 4        Monotony    1.44    1.448853
#> 5          Strain 5397.00 5396.975613

The monotony is 1.449. Foster prints 1.44: the value is truncated, not rounded. The printed strain, 5397, is computed from the unrounded monotony (MODELS.md, discrepancy log).

Limitations

  • Foster 1998 is an observational study of 25 athletes; thresholds were individual and chosen after the fact to explain illnesses; they are not validated cut-offs.
  • In that study, 52% of the excursions above the monotony threshold and 59% of those above the strain threshold were not followed by illness.
  • Monotony divides by a standard deviation: it is unstable when the days of the week are similar and undefined when they are equal; a single rest day changes it substantially.
  • The result depends on whether rest days count as zero. Foster does not say; this package counts them.
  • Session RPE load is in arbitrary units and is not comparable across athletes without care.
